armF.summary: Meta rolled back Muse’s test using human contractors to make calls after admitting it began without proper disclosure.
armF.prompt:
Below is a finished English news feature article (already translated from Japanese, no section headings). Write ONE short, natural sentence that captures the core of the story, in a way a listener can understand by hearing it just once.

Requirements:
- Exactly one sentence.
- Understandable on a single listen.
- Do not pack in multiple separate points; focus on the single most important point or twist of the story.
- Do not add any new fact, conclusion, or lesson that is not already stated in the article below.
- Keep who did what to whom, and what exactly it applied to, the same as in the Japanese source article and the Ledger below.

As a rough guide only (Trial-only guidance, not a strict rule): aim for one main clause with at most one subordinate clause, roughly 12-18 words.

Output only the sentence itself, nothing else (no quotation marks, no label like "In one line:", no Markdown heading markup).

[Article]
# A Surprising Human Helper for AI Phone Calls

When people asked AI to make a phone call, a human helper appeared backstage. That was the unexpected turn in tests of Meta’s consumer AI, Muse. Reports say Muse’s phone feature can call businesses and stores in the US to book a haircut, check stock, or ask a service provider for an estimate. On some of those calls, trained contract workers—not AI—made the calls and completed the conversations. AI took the request, and a human carried it out by phone. Before anyone knew it, the roles in the team handling the calls had changed.

This human helper brought more than convenience. If user information was needed to move a call forward, how much of it would be shared? Meta employees raised privacy concerns inside the company, saying that sensitive information might be shared by mistake with contract workers at call centers. The issue is not only what AI knows, but also what information is passed to the people who take over the job.

Then there is the question of explaining what is happening. Meta leaders admitted that starting tests in which contract workers made calls without proper disclosure was a “mistake,” and rolled back the human concierge feature. They stopped that feature, not Muse as a whole. How should users be told who is making the call? If a person is involved, how should their information be handled? If the roles change, an explanation needs to come with them.

Meta says it will keep improving the phone feature with businesses, and will release it only when it is ready and proper disclosure is possible. Users can ask AI to book appointments, check stock, or request estimates from stores and businesses in the US. If there is a person behind this convenience, it also matters how that person and the information they handle are treated, and how users are told about it. An AI service that makes calls is not complete just because it is smart on screen. Perhaps the curtain can rise with confidence only once the backstage details are settled too.

[Japanese source article]
AIの電話代行に、まさかの人間助っ人

AIに電話を頼んだら、舞台裏から人間の助っ人が登場。Metaの個人向けAI、Museをめぐるテストは、そんな展開でした。Museの電話機能では、米国内の企業や店舗に電話し、散髪の予約や在庫確認、業者からの見積もりを頼めると報じられています。その電話の一部では、AIではなく、訓練を受けた契約スタッフが電話をかけ、相手とのやり取りを完了させていました。AIが依頼を受け、人間が電話で実行する。代行チームの配役が、いつの間にか変わっていたわけです。

この人間の助っ人、便利なだけでは終わりません。電話を進めるためにユーザー情報が必要な場合、その情報がどこまで共有されるのか。Metaの従業員は、機微な情報がコールセンターの契約スタッフへ意図せず共有される可能性があるとして、社内でプライバシー上の懸念を示しました。問題はAIが何を知っているかだけではなく、仕事を引き継ぐ人に何が渡るのか、ということです。

そしてもうひとつ、説明の問題。適切な開示がないまま契約スタッフが電話するテストを始めたことについて、Meta幹部は「ミス」だったと認め、人間コンシェルジュ機能をロールバックしました。止めたのはその機能で、Muse全体ではありません。誰が電話しているのかをどう伝えるか。人が関わるなら情報をどう扱うか。配役を変えるなら、説明もセットで必要だったわけです。

Metaは電話機能について商業者との改善を続け、準備が整い、適切な開示ができる場合にだけ公開するとしています。米国内の店や企業への予約、在庫確認、見積もり依頼をAIに任せる。そんな便利さの舞台裏に人間がいるなら、その人と情報をどう扱い、利用者にどう伝えるかも大切です。AIの代行サービスは、画面の中の賢さだけでは完成しません。舞台裏まで決まって、ようやく安心して幕が上がるのかもしれません。

armR.final_summary: Meta rolled back Muse’s human concierge feature after admitting it was a mistake to let contractors make calls without proper disclosure.
armR.final_text:
# A Surprising Human Helper for AI Phone Calls

When people asked AI to make a phone call, a human helper appeared backstage. That was the unexpected turn in tests of Meta’s consumer AI, Muse. Reports say Muse’s phone feature can call businesses and stores in the US to book a haircut, check stock, or ask a service provider for an estimate. On some of those calls, trained contract workers—not AI—made the calls and completed the conversations. AI took the request, and a human carried it out by phone. Before anyone knew it, the roles in the team handling the calls had changed.

This human helper brought more than convenience. If user information was needed to move a call forward, how much of it would be shared? Meta employees raised privacy concerns inside the company, saying that sensitive information might be shared by mistake with contract workers at call centers. The issue is not only what AI knows, but also what information is passed to the people who take over the job.

Then there is the question of explaining what is happening. Meta leaders admitted that starting tests in which contract workers made calls without proper disclosure was a “mistake,” and rolled back the human concierge feature. They stopped that feature, not Muse as a whole. How should users be told who is making the call? If a person is involved, how should their information be handled? If the roles change, an explanation needs to come with them.

Meta says it will keep improving the phone feature with businesses, and will release it only when it is ready and proper disclosure is possible. Users can ask AI to book appointments, check stock, or request estimates from stores and businesses in the US. If there is a person behind this convenience, it also matters how that person and the information they handle are treated, and how users are told about it. An AI service that makes calls is not complete just because it is smart on screen. Perhaps the curtain can rise with confidence only once the backstage details are settled too.

## In one line
Meta rolled back Muse’s human concierge feature after admitting it was a mistake to let contractors make calls without proper disclosure.
